newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil creates human rights watchdog.
newsitem.headline: Brazil creates human rights watchdog.

text.p: Brazil on Monday set up a human rights watchdog to oversee human rights following widespread outrage over police brutality.

Officials said President Fernando Henrique Cardoso had signed a decree establishing the National Human Rights Secretariat and had also sanctioned a bill, recently passed by Congress, that makes torture a crime for the first time.

"We want to show the country that we must make more and more progress in this area (of human rights) and that we are not happy with what was often a lack of action in the past," Cardoso said as he signed the decree.

The creation of a human rights watchdog and the sanctioning of the torture law were rushed through following televised videotape footage last week of Sao Paulo military police beating up civilians, extorting money and allegedly killing a man.

Ten officers have been arrested and charged with a variety of crimes. The police violence, which rights groups say is commonplace, sparked general public anger and disgust, both in Brazil and overseas.

The new Human Rights Secretariat, to be headed by former Justice Ministry chief of staff Jose Gregori, a respected campaigner for civil rights, will oversee the implementation of a landmark National Plan for Human Rights.

Gregori said it would also esablish a commission to decide the future of the military police, a legacy of past military regimes and renowned for their violence. Critics say the military police should be amalgamated with civil police forces.
"Serious corrections are needed which cannot be undertaken in the heat of the moment," Gregori told reporters.

Asked why more action should be expected of Brazil now than in the past, Gregori said: "What's different now is that there is a political will to change the situation, no matter who may be offended in the process."

The filmed evidence of police brutality in Sao Paulo has breathed new life into many human rights projects which had become bogged down in Congress because of the opposition of powerful lobby groups, including that of the military police.

Traditionally, Brazil's military police have been tried by military courts for suspected crimes. Human rights groups and critics claim military courts are excessively lenient to their own, allowing the police to enjoy widespread impunity.

Backed by public outrage, the government hopes to send back to Congress a bill transferring crimes committed by military police to civil courts. The Senate had watered the bill down to apply only to crimes of homicide.

In addition, the government is pressing the Chamber of Deputies to approve a bill that would make crimes against human rights subject to federal justice, allowing the federal police to intervene and investigate.
